data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The two-standard-deviation fairness criterion itself is the wrong test: even for a perfectly fair generator, the probability that ALL six face counts fall within two sigma is only about 95% per face, so the joint probability is roughly 0.95^6 \u2248 0.735 \u2014 meaning a 'fair' generator fails this test about 26% of the time, making it a poor discriminator.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The six counts are sufficiently correlated that the joint probability of all being within two sigma is actually much higher than 0.954^6, making the test reasonable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The problem's definition of fairness is stipulative and binding regardless of its statistical power: the simulation returns counts and the criterion is applied as stated.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The problem defines fairness as every count falling within two standard deviations of the expectation. For a multinomial with n=10000, p=1/6, the counts are correlated (they sum to 10000). The probability that any single count is within 2 sigma is approximately 0.954 (normal approximation), but for six correlated counts the joint probability of all being within bounds is substantially less than 0.954. Thus, even a truly fair generator would frequently fail this criterion, and using it to classify this specific LCG output is epistemically questionable. The simulation should return the counts, but the fairness verdict requires a better statistical framework.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
